what: The Text to Binary tool turns normal text into binary code, the 0s and 1s that a computer really stores, and turns binary code back into text. Each byte is shown as a group of 8 digits, separated by spaces.

It helps students learning how computers store text, teachers preparing lessons, puzzle makers and developers who want to see the exact bytes of a string. Use it to check how many bytes a word takes, to decode a binary message, or to make a fun secret note.
The conversion runs in your browser and nothing is uploaded. Text is stored as UTF-8, so every language and emoji is supported.
uses: Type a word and see the 8-digit pattern for each letter, for example H is 01001000.
Paste a string of 0s and 1s from a puzzle, a T-shirt or a homework task and read the hidden text.
The message under the buttons tells you how many bytes the text uses, which is useful for size limits.
Type accented letters or emoji to see that they use 2, 3 or 4 bytes instead of 1.
Create binary exercises for students and check their answers by decoding.
tutorial: Click in the “Text or binary” box. Type normal text, or paste binary such as 01001000 01101001.
Click “Text to binary” to convert the text. Each byte appears as 8 digits, with one space between bytes. The message shows how many bytes there are, for example “3 bytes.”.
To go the other way, put binary in the box and click “Binary to text”. Spaces and line breaks are ignored, so 0100100001101001 works as well as 01001000 01101001.
If the binary has other characters, or the number of digits is not a multiple of 8, a red message explains the problem and how many digits it found.
Click “Copy” to copy the whole box to your clipboard.
Click “Clear” to empty the box and the message before the next conversion.
features: Convert text to binary and binary back to text in the same box.
All languages, accented letters and emoji are converted to their real UTF-8 bytes.
After converting to binary, the message tells you the exact number of bytes.
Spaces and line breaks between digits are ignored when decoding.
You are told if there are characters other than 0 and 1, if the digits are not in groups of 8, or if the bytes are not valid text.
One click copies the result or empties the box.

example.title: Worked example: the word Hi!
example.text: Type Hi! and click “Text to binary”. The box shows 01001000 01101001 00100001 and the message says “3 bytes.”. H is 72 in decimal, which is 01001000 in binary, i is 105 or 01101001, and ! is 33 or 00100001. Now click “Binary to text” and the box shows Hi! again. If you type the single letter é instead, you get 11000011 10101001 and “2 bytes.”, because UTF-8 needs two bytes for this letter.

tips: Each group of 8 digits is one byte, not always one character. Letters outside basic English use 2 to 4 bytes.
Spaces in your text are converted too. A space is 00100000.
When you paste binary, check that the total number of digits is divisible by 8. A missing digit at the start of a group shifts everything.
To read the number for each byte, convert it in a binary-to-decimal tool or count place values 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1.
Clicking “Text to binary” twice converts the binary digits themselves into binary. Click “Binary to text” once to undo it.
problems: The box has other characters, such as letters, commas or the digit 2, or it is empty. Remove them and try again.
“Binary text must be in groups of 8 digits.”
The message shows how many digits were found. A digit is missing or extra somewhere. Check each group has exactly 8 digits.
The digits form bytes that are not valid UTF-8, for example only part of a multi-byte letter. Check that you copied every group.
One wrong digit changes a letter completely. Compare the groups with the source carefully.
